research.query: How fast does a detector see smoke in microgravity?
research.answer:
The question was matched to: microgravity, smoke, smoke detection. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- SAME: Detectors must be checked against microgravity smoke, not Earth smoke. SAME was designed around the hypothesis that, without buoyant flows, smoke particles from pyrolysing materials grow larger than in 1 g; SAME and SAME-R provide quantitative data on detector sensitivity to… [S1]
- SAME-R: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-2: Comparison of Flight Experiment Results with Ground Test Results; Evaluation of Low-Gravity Smoke Particulate for Spacecraft Fire Detection; Particle Morphology and Size Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-2;… [S2]
- SAME: Quantified the size of smoke particulate produced in low gravity and how it relates to generation and transport conditions — baseline data for spacecraft smoke-detector sensitivity. [S3]
- SAME-R: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke. [S4]
- DAFT / DAFT-2: A Research Plan for Fire Prevention, Detection and Suppression in Crewed Exploration Systems; Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a f [S11]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.

sources.text: Detectors must be checked against microgravity smoke, not Earth smoke. SAME was designed around the hypothesis that, without buoyant flows, smoke particles from pyrolysing materials grow larger than in 1 g; SAME and SAME-R provide quantitative data on detector sensitivity to reduced-gravity smoke. sources.title: Microgravity and 1-g rankings of materials can disagree
sources.text: In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone samples (0.27–1.03 mm) had a burn length of about 0 in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while 2 of the 4 matching 1-g reference burns were complete. Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). Limitation: One test per configuration; single flow speed and near-normal O2.

sources.title: Stopping ventilation may not be enough in oxygen-enriched cabins
sources.text: In quiescent microgravity, BRE flames emulating condensed materials (e.g. PMMA, nylon) kept burning quasi-steadily in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas comparable flames at 21 % O2 self-extinguished in a short time. PSI describes these results as preliminary. Limitation: Gaseous emulation of solids; per-test pressure not in the summary table; results flagged preliminary.

top_passage.text: The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point.
